What is the commonality of the accomplishments, and what is their supreme form?
How many kinds of means are there therein, and what is the goal to be attained like? (20)
How do the yogins issue commands to all the Vajra-holders? How do they produce diversity? Tell me all that quickly. (21)

Then all those Tathāgatas, having heard the words of inquiry from those Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, remained silent for a moment, focusing their attention upon the Great Bodhisattva Mahāvajradhara. Then all those Great Bodhisattvas, joyful and compassionate in nature, exhorted the Perfect Buddhas, the Sugatas, the Protectors, again and again: 22. Then all those Great Bodhisattvas, joyful and compassionate in nature, exhorted the Perfect Buddhas, the Sugatas, the Protectors, again and again.

Then all those Tathāgatas spoke thus to those Bodhisattvas: "O lords of Bodhisattvas, you who possess the vajra of body, speech, and mind, listen through the vajra of body, speech, and mind to the detailed questions for the sake of sentient beings. (23)

Then all those great bodhisattvas, having received the words of favor from all those Tathāgatas, focused their own body, speech, and mind-vajras upon the body, speech, and mind-vajra of the Great Bodhisattva Mahāvajradhara, and remained silent, saying, "Excellent, excellent, O Blessed Ones! Excellent, excellent, O Sugatas!
Thereupon, all those Tathāgatas, whose nature is great compassion, focused within their hearts and empowered those great bodhisattvas, and with one voice they explained those questions.
The threefold body, speech, and mind are designated as the "secret. "Assembly" (samāja) is said to mean "gathering," which is the designation for all Buddhas. (24)
The fifth, the ninth, the tenth, the seventh, and the thirteenth:
this is the great teaching and practice of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. (25)
The fourth, the sixteenth, the eighth, and likewise the twelfth:
these are the common duties of the teacher; success indeed arises from the observance of the vows.
The eighth, the second, the tenth, the fifteenth, and the fourteenth; these are the Haṭha, Anurāgaṇa, Upasādhana, and Saṃvara [observances]. (27)
The seventh and the third, the tenth, eleventh, and fifth;
these are the signs of the field of accomplishment, as well as the commitment of service and practice.
The activity of all Tathāgatas, capable of both subduing and favoring, is the very means of delivering sentient beings—whether they be self-controlled, difficult to tame, or gentle. (29)
The connection with the stage of generation consists of four vajra-rituals of service.
The ripening of disciples by means of the mantra path through the gurus. || 30 ||
For the high-souled disciple of excellent vows who has been consecrated, there is the teaching and liberation [granted] by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. (31)
The meditative union of wisdom and means is designated as "yoga.
Wisdom, by its very nature, is the source, while means is the characteristic of existence. (32)

The treatise (tantra) is declared to be a continuous composition (prabandha), and that continuous composition is threefold, according to the divisions of the basis (ādhāra), the nature (prakṛti), and the indestructible (asaṃhārya). || 33 ||
The nature of form, its cause, likewise its indestructible fruit, its support, and the means for that—by these three, the summary of the meaning of the Tantra is comprised. (34)
The pentad, the triple family, and the hundred families of intrinsic nature—this simultaneous teaching on the Bodhivajra is held to be the *Uttaratantra*. (35)
Reality is declared to be the five families; the secret is said to be the three families. The presiding deity is the mystery, and the supreme family is a hundredfold.
Without beginning or end, peaceful, the inexhaustible beyond existence and non-existence, all-pervasive, and indivisible from emptiness and compassion—this is known as bodhicitta. (37)
Because his nature is both penetrable and impenetrable by means of the vajras of body, speech, and mind, he who is united with the vidyā is called the Vidyāpuruṣa. || 38 ||
The five *hetis* and *vetīs* are designated as the *vajra*;
their retention is known as *dhṛk*, and the consciousness that holds the *vajra* is the mind (*manas*). (39)
The body of all sentient beings is known as the middle way, arising from the primary elements and their derivatives; it is the Victor, the progenitor of the Conquerors and the Conquered. 40.
The mind is known as the "accumulated jewel," arising from all objects;
it is the certain knower, that which is to be known, and feeling is the mind that holds the jewel. 41.
Through the relationship of the characterized and the characteristic, everything is everywhere and by everything;
the characteristic is delight, and the characterized is said to be the *āmaroli*. || 42 ||
That consciousness which is produced by excellence is called wisdom (prajñā);
that which sustains the volition of formative forces (saṃskāra-cetanā) is termed the "wisdom-sustainer" (prajñā-dhṛk). || 43 ||
The lineage is declared to be the succession; by means of the successions, the beginning is spoken of. That which is indestructible and unarisen is proclaimed as the Name.
Consciousness is declared to be hatred, for it gives and takes through the duality of the hateful;
form is known as delusion, by virtue of its nature as a dull bondage. (45)
Feeling (vedanā) is called "striking" because its nature is ego-grasping (ahaṅkāra);
perception (saṃjñā) is essentially characterized by passion and the power of objective representation. (46)
But conditioned formations are always envy, by virtue of their nature as that which impels; whereas the essence of the mind of awakening (bodhicitta) arises everywhere throughout existence. 47.
Desire is said to be the mind accompanied by passion, hatred, and delusion; it is the commitment (samaya) directed toward the appearance of the universe, the fruit born of karma. 48.
Envy regarding the phenomena of non-dual gnosis is called delusion (moha);
the mutual friction [of thoughts] therein is designated as hatred (dveṣa). || 49 ||
The characteristic of passion is attachment; this wisdom is called the vajra.
Delight is the ultimate enjoyment, and the bliss of women is the supreme attainment. (50)
Delusion, hatred, and likewise passion—delight always resides in the vajra.
Therefore, it is known as the Vajrayāna, the means of the Buddhas. (51)
Phenomena are non-destructible by nature because they are unarisen;
therefore, the Lord of Death, who brings an end to all beings, is himself that very commitment (samaya). 52.
Phenomena are non-conscious by nature from the perspective of ultimate purity;
this is the commitment (*samaya*) of all minds, and therefore the Victor is the one who brings wisdom to its end.
Phenomena are inexpressible in nature; they are the cognition of non-existence, namelessness, and formlessness.
He is the convention of all phenomena; therefore, the Lord is the one who brings about the end of the lotus.
All phenomena are non-conceptual by nature, for their essence is inherently peaceful;
therefore, he is the Lord who brings an end to obstacles, the commitment of all Vajras.
This knowledge of the awakening of the Buddhas is indestructible, unknowable, ineffable, and non-conceptual; having realized this, one attains happiness. (56)
Through the enjoyment of delusion, one becomes free from the delusion of destruction;
by that, one becomes the ender of the body, and likewise the ender of the knowable. 57.

A fault is exhausted by the experience of that fault; thus, one who brings an end to faults brings about the end of wisdom, brings about the end of the mind, and likewise brings about the end of the afflictions. 58.

Passion, through the enjoyment of passion, becomes the passion of exhaustion; it brings about the end of the lotus, and by that means, it likewise brings about the end of speech and the end of meditative absorption. (59)
That which is the exhaustion of all afflictions is likewise the exhaustion of all karma;
this knowledge, which is the exhaustion of all obscurations, is known as the "End-maker of Obstacles. (60)
When purified within the enclosure of the vajra of afflictions, all action is completely purified;
because all action is purified, the fruit born of action is pure. (61)
Grasping, attachment, and likewise immovability of form,
as well as the state of being a cause and the state of being a fruit— the arising of the mind occurs through these six.

The six groups beginning with Ṭakkirāja are renowned as the Lords of Wrath (krodhendras); they are celebrated as the elements and their derivatives, and are renowned as the Kings of Knowledge (vidyārājas). || 63 ||
The six beginning with Rūpavajrā are known as the Vajra Lords; the five beginning with Samayavajrā reside within the [elements] beginning with earth. (64)
From the vajras of mind, speech, and body, the Great Being arises;
his form consists of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, produced from wisdom and skillful means.

Having ascertained this through yoga, the mantra-practitioner, by means of the yoga of the completion stage (niṣpannakrama), should be free from all fear through the resolute conviction (adhimokṣa) in the purity of all things. || 66 ||
The practitioner of mantra should roam like a lion with a mind free from hesitation;
for here there is nothing that should not be done, and likewise nothing that should not be eaten.
There is nothing that cannot be expressed, and there is always nothing that cannot be conceived.
Through the yoga of non-concentration, he is eternally concentrated. || 68 ||
The conduct that exists within all thoughts is called universal conduct.
Whatever arises dependently through the sense faculties, their objects, and the mind.
That mind is known as "manas" because of its nature as the agent of thought and its purpose of protection.
That which is called the commitment-restraint (samayasamvara) is entirely free from worldly conduct.
The protection by means of all the vajras is called the practice of mantra.
Having investigated each respective intrinsic nature with the mind within the heart.
As for the recitation (japa), it consists of the emanation and withdrawal [of the mantra], by uttering the mantra according to its divisions.
One should dissolve the Buddhas, whose nature is the universal vajra, by means of the seed-syllable of gnosis. || 72 ||
The practitioner, by means of the seed-syllable of the selflessness of awakening, should meditate upon [the deity] as being without self.
One should expand the universe like the universal [mantra], and recite that with the seed-syllable of the three times.
Recitation (japa) is declared to be speaking; it is said that all speech is mantra.
"Mantra" is declared to be that which is spoken as an exhortation; it is the reality itself. || 74 ||
Just as there is the empowerment of the heart and likewise meditative absorption, so too is there the consecration upon their crowns and worship in every respect. || 75 ||
For him who possesses the yoga known through knowledge, together with that of the Vajra-holder, his enjoyments are to be understood as fourfold, such as self-consecration and the rest. (76)
For each one of the heroes with a single face, there is a consecration upon the head;
by means of the heart-mudrā and the path of mantra, they are sealed according to the traditions of their own families.
Having sealed the cause with the fruit and having sealed the fruit with the cause, one should meditate; otherwise, accomplishment will not arise even in ten million eons. (78)
One should visualize the Vidyāpuruṣa, the wielder of the vajra, endowed with the four enjoyments, distributed among the three triangles according to the division of body, speech, and mind. (79)
One should visualize a ten-spoked wheel that has been turned inward; in its center, one should contemplate the ten wrathful deities arising as the essence of the ten gnoses upon each spoke.
One should meditate with the completed Nirodha-cakra, most excellent and beautiful,
emitting clouds of vajra-flames that swirl like something motionless.
Thus, the primordial wisdom of the source of phenomena (dharmodaya) is by nature stainless and auspicious;
through its cultivation for even a single moment, the Buddha-eye is produced.
The teaching for the Vajra-holders therein relies upon two stages:
namely, the stage of generation and likewise the stage of completion. (83)
The means of accomplishment, the practice, and likewise the commitment and restraint—all of these are previously explained in detail according to their various sequential divisions. (84)
Sensual desires, such as forms, sounds, and so forth, consist of pleasure, pain, and both.
They constantly produce in the heart the arising of passion, hatred, and delusion. || 85 ||
In passion, there is a vajra consisting of passion, born from the Vajra-Jewel; the pledge (samaya) arises like a jewel, and those desires are comparable to the pledge. || 86 ||
Having a form and being formless, all-pervading and consisting of the three syllables, one should perform the acts of taking up, withdrawing, and expanding through one's own recitation. 87.
Thus, having produced hatred and delusion throughout the three worlds and having sealed them,
the Vajrins accomplish the purpose that is purified in secret.
Having produced the wheel of hatred through the yoga of hatred for the practitioners,
one should incinerate it with the fierce vajra and then dissolve it within the wielder of the wisdom-vajra.
Having expanded those [rays] and awakened them, one should practice the yoga of their reabsorption again; in this way, one will personally become Dveṣavajra.
He brings about both death and life throughout the three realms without exception in a mere instant; his power is manifest, there is no doubt. 91.
Having produced the wheel of delusion through the yoga of delusion, the yogi should always impel all things whatsoever, such as ornaments and the like. 92.
One should meditate upon the ocean of deluded mind as filled with all jewels;
it shall rain down a shower of gifts for all those who possess the wheel of delusion.
Indeed, with a mind made firm by the vajra, he performs the giving and taking of all substances without exception in a mere instant. (94)
Having generated the wheel of passion through the yoga of passion,
the yogin should take it away from all the gods and desire them by means of the yoga of desire.
Then, with the delights of passion, pleasure, and joy, manifested through amorous play,
the entire wheel-bearer should offer [the oblation] to the five deities.
Even the gods and asuras desire for a mere moment a wife born within the three realms; how much more so, then, human women? (97)
The mandala initiation, the various sequences of ritual actions, the performance, the empowerment, and the destination of those who have attained accomplishment—otherwise [it would not be so]. (98)
The *bhaga* is called the mandala, and the *bodhicitta* is the mandala;
the body is said to be the mandala—thus is the conceptualization of the three mandalas. (99)
Everything is sealed by the seal of the aggregates, sense-bases, and elements;
therefore, one should designate that the seal is always applied as the mandala. (100)
One should place the goad, the staff-trident, and the sword in the corners;
and below and above, one should place Ṭakki, Daṇḍabala, Bāla, the discus, and Sumbha.

The mudrās of the Vidyārājas and other Vajras, as well as those of the six Cakravartins, and the respective mudrā-maṇḍalas of sentient beings within the elements such as earth and so forth—[these are described]. (102)
A mirror, a lute, a conch, a vessel, and likewise images on cloth—
this is the mudrā known as Dharmodayā, belonging to the Vajra-holders who are the Lords of the Vajra.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are sealed by the Wrathful Kings;
others, however, are single heroes (ekavīra) designated according to their family color. || 104 ||
The self-natures (*svadhātu*) of young women are designated as "flowers.
One should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) according to the lineages of the families (*kulakrama*), through the divisions of body, speech, and mind. (105)
The *caitya* of all Buddhas is called the place of the abode;
that which is emanated by the *jñānasattva* is known as the *jñānacakra*. (106)
The seed-syllable phrase is proclaimed as the imperishable syllable of the three vajras;
it is proclaimed as the impelling and the awakening through the nature of body, speech, and mind. (107)
The impelling is the movement of rays throughout the world-systems of the ten directions; the summoning is the invitation of all vajra-holders, the universal invitation to the vajras. (108)
Having withdrawn all vajras into that state by means of the ray of light of all vajras, their binding in the form of a mass is called "bondage. (109)
Having sealed body, speech, and mind with the vajra of body, speech,
and mind within the mandala of body, speech, and mind, one should fashion the painted mandala.
In this tantra, initiation is prescribed as having three divisions:
the first is the vase initiation, and the second is from the secret initiation. (111)
The third is the gnosis of wisdom (*prajñājñāna*), and the fourth is likewise that same [gnosis].
[One should worship] the wide-eyed consort suitable for mantra, who possesses flowers and is born from semen. (112)
One should bestow the secret and most secret initiation upon the disciple who is a mantra-practitioner,
having placed [the substances] within the center of the space-element, combined with feces, urine, and marrow.
By means of the application of the vajra and lotus, one should assemble all vajras;
having caused them all to descend into the heart from the vajras of body, speech, and mind. || 114 ||
Having emitted it through the path of the vajra, one should cause it to fall into the mouth of the disciple.
This is the supreme state of consecration for all vajras. 115.
All mantras and the various successions of supreme rites are accomplished [by her who is] exceedingly faithful, of great wisdom, beautiful in form, and dear to the practitioner. 116.
Having indeed beheld the initiate who has practiced the ritual of the single yoga, the practitioner must certainly offer a sacrificial fee to the guru. (117)
Having been requested by the Guru, that [initiation] should be bestowed upon the practitioner;
for the deluded one, the yoga consisting of delusion, accompanied by delight in delusion, should be given. 118.
Through the continuous flow of delusions, one becomes Mohavajra himself;
toward the hateful, one should employ the yoga consisting of hatred, conjoined with delight in hatred. (119)
From the sprinkling of streams of hatred, the Vajra of Hatred shall be on the right;
when it is red, the yoga is of the nature of passion, endowed with the delight of passion. (120)
From the continuous flow of passion, one becomes Rāgavajra himself;
this yoga, consisting of the knowledge of wisdom (prajñājñāna), is endowed with vajra-delight.
Through the consecration by streams of gnosis, one becomes the wisdom-knowledge (*prajñājñāna*) itself;
having taken that very deity, the *vidyā*, [one bestows it] upon the disciple who holds the vajra. 122.
The hand should be placed upon the hand, having called the Tathāgatas to witness;
by placing his hand upon the head of the disciple, the Guru-Vajrī releases him. 123.
Buddhahood is not attained by any other means; therefore, this supreme vidyā is the best.
All phenomena are non-dual, yet they are characterized by the appearance of duality. 124.
Therefore, you must never bring about separation within cyclic existence;
this is the unsurpassed vow of knowledge of all the Buddhas. (125)
The fool who transgresses this does not attain success, as it has been said;
by its very nature, the fivefold impurity shines forth within the attributes of the body. (126)
Because it is empowered by the five gnoses, it is known as the "five nectars.
It consists of blazing, heating, illuminating, and the perception of form. 127.
Through the application of the mantra-form, one should consume the nectar of the five nectars;
one should contemplate it as being situated in the intermediate space, arising from the vajra-hūṃ syllable. 128.
Below that part, however, one should place in the center the nectar arising in the form of a lotus, marked with the syllable Oṃ.
Having ignited and heated it through the union of the vajra and lotus, the yogin raises [it], which has the appearance of crystal like another sun of gnosis. (130)
Having drawn [the nectar] from the world-systems of the ten directions by means of the supreme weapon,
one should pour that nectar there and consume it through the yoga of consumption.
Likewise, the fivefold hero’s food (pañcavīrya) is to be consumed according to the rules for accomplishing the desired goal;
it must be prepared with the three-syllable seed-mantras, for otherwise they do not bestow accomplishment.
The supernatural powers such as invisibility and so forth are proclaimed to be common attainments;
however, the Buddhas have declared that the supreme attainment is the means for achieving Buddhahood. (133)
One should attain the fourfold increase as described by Bodhivajra; it is always praised by the yogin in all the Yoga Tantras. (134)

The first is the rite of service (sevāvidhāna), the second is the near-attainment (upasādhana), the third is indeed the attainment (sādhana), and the fourth is the great attainment (mahāsādhana). || 135 ||
Service is of two kinds, distinguished as common and supreme:
the common is performed with the four vajras, and the supreme with the nectar of gnosis.
The first is the awakening to emptiness; the second is the gathering of the seed-syllable;
the third is the accomplishment of the image; and the fourth is the placement of the immutable syllable.
By means of these four vajras, the common practice of service (sevā) is to be performed through the six-limbed yoga within the supreme nectar of gnosis. || 138 ||
Having performed the supreme practice through the yoga of the six-limbed service, one should accomplish [the goal];
otherwise, the supreme siddhi will certainly not arise. 139.
Withdrawal of the senses, meditation, breath control, concentration, recollection, and absorption—this is said to be the six-limbed yoga. (140)
The withdrawal of the ten sense organs from all their respective objects of activity for the sake of attaining mastery over them is called *pratyāhāra*. 141.
The five sense-pleasures, in brief, through the application of the five Buddhas, are called "meditative concentration" (dhyāna); that meditative concentration is of five kinds. (142)
Initial application, sustained application, joy, bliss,
and one-pointedness of mind— these five are the constituents of dhyāna.
In all the secret tantras, various [types of] reasoning are proclaimed: secret reasoning, arising reasoning, and analytical reasoning through its application. (144)
The third is like joy, the fourth is the gathering of bliss;
one's own mind is to be known as the fifth, which is knowledge, the object of knowledge, and patient compassion. 145.
Consisting of all Buddhas, peaceful, and established in all desires;
the breath consists of the five gnoses and has the nature of the five elements. (146)
Having emitted it in the form of a globule, one should visualize it at the tip of the nose as a great jewel of five colors; this is known as *prāṇāyāma*.
Having meditated on one's own mantra within the heart, one should place it as having entered the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the point (*bindu*).
Having restrained the sense-faculties and holding the jewel, this is known as *dhāraṇā* (retention). 148.
When the mind has entered the vajra of cessation, a sign arises;
that sign is fivefold, as taught by the Bodhivajra. (149)
The first has the appearance of a mirage; the second, the appearance of smoke;
the third, the appearance of a firefly; and the fourth, blazing like a lamp. 150.
The fifth, however, is constant light, cloudless and resembling the sky;
one should expand it steadily through the path of the vajra within the elements of space.
Having meditated upon that which is to be recollected, one should clearly recollect its very form;
this is to be known as "recollection" (anusmṛti), for a vivid manifestation arises therein. 152.
Having condensed all phenomena in brief through the meditative union of wisdom and means, one should visualize them within the central image by means of the yoga of the mass. 153.
The instantaneous perfection of knowledge is designated as "samādhi";
having attained withdrawal (pratyāhāra), one is empowered by all mantras.
Having entered the meditative knowledge of dhyāna, one shall attain the state of the five superknowledges;
through breath control (prāṇāyāma), one is certainly empowered by the Bodhisattvas.
Through the constant power of *dhāraṇā*, Vajrasattva enters [the practitioner];
through the union of *anusmṛti*, a circle of light arises. (156)
Merely by attaining mastery over meditative concentration, one becomes free from obscurations;
that mind, having been focused upon in the heart through the application of the four vajras, [becomes so]. (157)
Having drawn forth the mind with the supreme weapon and made it consist of mantra,
one should recite the verse of awakening through the application of the mantra-form.
Mounted upon the maṇḍala of the lunar disk through the meditations on the union with awakening, that mind, by means of the image of gnosis, is the meditation of the *upasādhana*. 159.
As long as there are two kinds of vision, so long must there be cultivation for six months;
one should always and in every way engage in the enjoyment of all desires.
If the vision that was described does not arise even after six months, one should begin again for three cycles according to the samvara rules as prescribed by the ritual. 161.
Even when practiced in this way, the vision does not arise for the practitioner;
when enlightenment is not accomplished, one should practice through haṭhayoga. (162)
Then his accomplishment of knowledge arises through yoga alone;
by means of the application of the division of families, one should pin [the opponent] with the vajra-stake. 163.
Then, one should perform the rite of subjugation and protection through the practical application;
having withdrawn the Knower of the Wheel (jñānacakrin) by means of the method of great passion (mahārāga). 164.
Having expanded the consort ninefold, one should place her within the body of the sādhya;
then, having transformed the four mudrās, one should fashion the maṇḍala therein.
Having placed [the deity] within oneself, one should withdraw all the wheel-bearers;
having made everything consist of vajra, one should then meditate upon awakening.
When the heart has been exhorted by the four goddesses with their songs of exhortation,
one should contemplate the body as an embodiment of gnosis, consisting of the vajra of the three times.
By intoxication the color is split, and likewise the heart by the flavor;
its own cause is through consecration, for the fruit arises from the differentiation of the substratum.
By means of mantra, leather is pierced; even knowledge [is mastered] by the Dharma-seal.
This [knowledge] has issued forth from the crown of the head (uṣṇīṣa) of the Universal Monarch of the six wheels. 169.

She is renowned as the Queen of Knowledge (Vidyārājñī), possessing four enjoyments and great supernatural power; she should be known as the fulfiller of all desires, as well as the sovereign of the Vajras. || 170 ||
The consecration of all [beings] by means of the meditation-vajra is praised;
through this application of the ritual, together with gnosis, [one attains] the body. 171.

The means of accomplishing the non-duality through the vajras of body, speech, and mind, according to the previously stated sequence, belongs to the Vajra-holder, the Knowledge-Person (vidyāpuruṣa). 172.
The emanation of the maṇḍala by one who possesses the self is called the Great Accomplishment (mahāsādhana).
At the time of service, one should rely upon the Bimba [deity] through yoga as the Great Uṣṇīṣa.

At the time of the *upasādhana*, the practitioner who knows the ritual procedure should perform the yoga of the deity with the image [of] Amṛtakuṇḍalī; during the *sādhana*, he should likewise do so. (174)
And at the time of the great accomplishment, this image of the all-pervading Lord Buddha is the secret of all Vajras for the supreme yogins. (175)
Thus, having understood through this distinction, one should accomplish the supreme siddhi;
otherwise, the highest auspiciousness of perfect accomplishment will never arise. 176.
Even in thousands of millions of eons, that which is the union of the goal and the means of the Buddhas, the Protectors, is called "service. (177)
The union of the vajra and the lotus is called the *upasādhana*;
the *sādhana* is said to be the movement accompanied by the syllables *hūṃ* and *phaṭ*. || 178 ||
The nature of space, the mouth of space, peaceful—this is called the Great Accomplishment;
it is the station of the glorious Lord of all Buddhas, the Great Vajradharas. (179)
She alone is the goal of all Buddhas and the very nature (dharmatā) of all phenomena;
for whatever action a yogin undertakes by relying upon yoga in accordance with its specific form, [she is the result]. 180.
Having constructed the mandala there, one should cause [the disciple] to hear the formidable pledge;
one should first protect the pledge of the Vajra-holder of body, speech, and mind. (181)
Alternatively, one who observes the *uṣṇīṣa* vow may grant the command of his own maṇḍala according to the specific rite described, in accordance with each respective ritual action. (182)
One should cause the person to be initiated to visualize his own body as the mandala;
furthermore, one should cause him to hear [the teachings] regarding those wheels (cakrin) residing within their bodies. 183.
Then, having caused them to fall [into that state], one should visualize them as having emerged;
drawing them in with one's entire being, one should cause them to enter one's own wheel.
Having fashioned an image of him from the aforementioned materials,
one should step upon the *liṅga* with the foot, while the mind is possessed by wrath.

Then, for the sake of subduing [the opponent], the Vajra-holder—the practitioner and the one to be accomplished—should dispatch the Krodhas who have received the command, surrounded by hosts of those fearless of their names. (186)
Bound, struck, and enveloped by that King of Wrath, the subject—tormented and seized with terror—is then drawn forth. || 187 ||
One should cause [the effigy] of that mantra-practitioner of the triple vajra to fall;
one should then stake it with the staking mantra at the head, the throat, and likewise the heart.
Having struck down calamities, afflictions, and diseases arising from various poisons into those images, one should likewise firmly pin them with stakes.
Then, by means of every application, according to the possible procedures as they have been described,
one should employ the diagrams, mantras, and so forth, according to the specific nature of the rite.

One should visualize oneself performing recitation while treading upon a *liṅga*, or performing fire-offerings within the *krodha* maṇḍala, or practicing meditation while being devoured by fierce creatures. (191)
In rites of pacification, one should have a peaceful mind; in rites of enrichment, a mind full of nourishment;
having made the mind red for subjugation, one should accomplish wrathful acts with a wrathful mind.
Thus [ends the verse]. || 192 ||

Then the Blessed Ones, all the Tathāgatas, having severed the doubts of those Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, took as their object through their own body, speech, and mind the one who severs all doubts— the Body, Speech, and Mind Vajra— who dwells within his own Body, Speech, and Mind Vajras, and remained silent. Then all those Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas praised those Tathāgatas with this King of Praises:
Homage to you in all your bodies; homage, homage to you in all your speech!
Homage to you in all your minds; homage, homage to you in the hearts of all beings! 193.

Because the vajras of body, speech, and mind are the very nature of body, speech, and mind, the Buddhas are equal to all beings; who is the object to be accomplished, and who is the practitioner? (194)
If the great-souled practitioner is not tainted by sins through the destruction of all Buddhas, how could he be tainted [otherwise]; and if he were tainted, how could there be a fruit? 195.

-136- Then all those Tathāgatas gave their approval to those great Bodhisattvas: "Excellent, excellent, O Great Beings! Excellent, excellent, O Great Sages! Excellent, excellent, O Great Voices! Excellent, excellent, O Great Festivals! (196)
The glorious Master, the sovereign of all Buddhas, possesses the vajra of awakening;
he is the agent of the creation and destruction of all phenomena, which are indeed like an illusion. (197)
For him there shall be neither sin nor likewise merit;
for one who has neither merit nor sin, awakening (bodhi) is proclaimed.
Deceiving that Protector is the destruction of all embodied beings;
yet for them, no miserable rebirth shall arise, and awakening will not be difficult to attain. 199.
If, due to a terrible deed committed in the past, hell arises for those beings, it results in a great fruit for those denizens of hell. (200)
They become sealed by wisdom; this is the goal of those who possess the vajra of enlightenment.
By that, it should be known as the supreme benefit for sentient beings of the yogins. 201.

The activity of subduing and favoring is the duty of those great-souled ones; having performed the rites up to the great accomplishment (*mahāsādhana*), one should then commence the ritual action. 202.

Then all those bodhisattva mahāsattvas, having heard the Dharma of the method of great compassion for all vajras, were pleased, thoroughly pleased, and completely satisfied, and they gave their approval, saying:
“Excellent, excellent, O Great Protectors! Excellent, excellent, O Great Sage!
Excellent, excellent, O Great Dharmas! Excellent, excellent, O Great Compassionate Ones! (203)
Oh, how the compassion of Samantabhadra is supremely pure, bestowing the fruit of Buddhahood even upon the wicked who commit cruel deeds! (204)
Then all those Tathāgatas said this to those Bodhisattvas, Mahāsattvas:

"Therefore, noble sons, a mantra-practitioner who has been consecrated in this *Sarvatathāgatābhiṣekaguhyasamāja* should not be terrified, should not be frightened, and should not fall into terror. Why is that?"
The great ones, such as Dveṣavajra and the others, who are born from the Bodhivajra—no rejection of them should be made in this continuous compendium of mantras. (205)
Then those Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas praised all those Tathāgatas with these verses in a single voice:

We constantly pay homage with body, mind, and speech to that which is the arising of the Vajra of the three times, which is both existence and liberation, peaceful, unobscured, and the nature of the pure realm of space—the Buddha, the Primordial Buddha, the Supreme Lord, the Bodhicitta-Vajra. (206)

Whatever form, sensation, perception, formations, and consciousness; the six bases and the six faculties; water, fire, wind, earth, and space—we bow to all of those vast ones who are like the mind of awakening. (207)

We pay homage to those vast [deities] who resemble the mind of awakening—those who are of the nature of the vajra-dharma, constantly produced through the application of vidyā-mantras, who are the supreme dharmas born of delusion, hatred, and likewise passion, and who have become the very essence of states overwhelmed by various and manifold delights. (208)

We pay homage to those vast Vajras, which are like the Vajra of Awakening: to gathering, delight, and likewise the immovable; to the dharmas that follow the mind’s nature regarding cause and fruit; and to delusion, fault, passion, and likewise obscuration. (209)
We always pay homage to those who meditate upon this pure, beginningless state, born of wisdom and skillful means, and beyond all comparison;
who are ever devoted to the yoga of the secret initiation, vows, and restraints—those we honor like the diamond of awakening itself. (210)

We always pay homage to those lords of practitioners who, through the service, near-attainment, and attainment, cultivate this supreme means for accomplishment; those masters of practice who are most certain in the great attainment—like the Vajra of Awakening, we take them as our goal. || 211 ||

Those who, by means of the vajras of the four performed junctures, accomplish various inferior siddhis such as invisibility and the like, and who—through the grace of the Buddha and the Guru—never lose this path: to them, like the Bodhivajra, we always pay homage a hundred thousand times. (212)

Those who hear this most secret tantra of the assembly, and who recite it, read it, contemplate it, perform worship, write it down, or cause it to be written—those we always honor with a hundredfold salutations, like the Vajra of Awakening itself. (213)

And those supreme lords of practitioners who are devoted to the private recitation of this [tantra], through the well-arranged expansion of rites for pacification and so forth, by means of the machine known through mantra and likewise sealed—we always bow to them, as if they were the diamond of awakening itself. (214)

Those who teach and touch [the name], those who remember and hear even the mere name of the Lord of Accomplishers, those who place their faith in him and dwell in a single place—we always bow to them, regarding them as the very essence of the Vajra of Awakening. 215.
With these peaceful words of praise, one should extend [protection] to all the leaders;
those lords, the Bodhisattvas of great majesty, will grant their approval.
This well-spoken tantra is the supreme sovereign of all tantras;
it is the Guhyasamāja of all Tathāgatas, born from the secret.
Thus [ends the section]. || 217 ||

Having spoken this, all those Tathāgatas and those Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, having taken as their object with their own body, speech, and mind the body, speech, and mind of the Body-Speech-Mind Vajra who dwells within the vajras of their own body,
speech, and mind, became silent.
Thus it is said.

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Empowerment of Vajra-Gnosis: The Instruction on All Secrets," from the *Śrī Guhyasamāja*, the Great King of Secret Tantras, which is the most secret of secrets concerning the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas.
This concludes the first half of the body of the *Śrī Guhyasamāja*, the King of Tantras. —139—
